remote-usability-studies.name: Remote Usability Studies
remote-usability-studies.desc: Use a sample pool of participants who match your target audience. Watch and listen as they walk through your site and perform tasks set by you, designed to emulate your core user journey or area of focus. Tasks and questions are set up within an external tool, meaning participants complete the session independently in their own time, thinking out loud as they go. Once complete, the recording of their screen, voice over (and sometimes webcam image) will be accessible within the tool for analysis.
remote-usability-studies.use: Gather insight into on-site friction points on a specific page, piece of functionality, core user journey, or full website. Uncovers key areas of confusion, frustration, and barriers to conversion. Gather data on metrics such as task success rate, time per task, System Usability Score, etc.
remote-usability-studies.pros: One of the key benefits of remote usability studies vs. moderated is that it is conducted from the comfort of the participant's own home, using their own devices. This helps make the session more realistic. The fact there is no moderator or live observers can also help prevent research bias such as the Hawthorne effect.
remote-usability-studies.cons: The remote nature of the sessions means that users can sometimes go "off track" or misunderstand the tasks, which can negatively impact or invalidate the insights and data. The lack of a moderator means there's no limited control over the session, including bringing the participant back on track or gathering more specific insights by asking specific and / or follow up questions.
remote-usability-studies.considerations:
Tool
There are many remote usability study tools, with slightly different capabilities and pricing models. Much like with AB testing tools, the success of your research is not necessarily determined by the tool you use, but by what you do with it (e.g. accurate recruitment, well-crafted tasks, and questions, etc). Key considerations when picking a tool include; the size and quality of their participant panel, the ability to add a recruitment screener, the analysis capabilities, what's included (e.g. participant incentives). Also double check how their pricing works, e.g. does it scale up based on the recruitment criteria and estimated length of session. 

Sample Size
Nielsen Norman says "The answer is 5, except when it's not" regarding usability study sample size. We use this as a guide; but one that should be considered rather than followed blindly. For example, if you're testing on multiple devices or with different user types, then you need to apply this rule to all of those segments. You may also want to add 1-2 additional "buffer" sessions to account for poorer quality participants, tech issues, no shows, etc.

customer-survey.name: Customer Survey
customer-survey.desc: A customer survey sent out via email to your customers (ideally segmented by customer type, e.g. new customers, recently lapsed customers, VIPs, etc). Typically the goal of a customer survey is to understand customers perception of your product/service, to understand what problem/s your product/service solves for them and any improvement areas based on their experiences.
customer-survey.use:
To understand customers motivations, FUDs (fears, uncertainties, and doubts) perception of your product/service, to understand what problem/s your product/service solves for them and any improvement areas based on their experiences. 

Customer surveys can also be used to investigate specific topics or areas of opportunity.
customer-survey.pros:
A customer survey allows you to gather large samples of data, which isn't possible when running customer interviews. Customer surveys can also be used alongside customer interviews to increase the depth of insight. 

Customer surveys can be used to gather valuable insight into wider business strategy, as well as what is important to users in general when considering products/services like yours. 

Customer surveys allow you to gather both qualitative and quantitative data, depending on the types of questions you ask.
customer-survey.cons:
An insightful customer survey is determined by the questions you ask. you need to avoid leading questions, and also ensure questions are not multifaceted as this can cause difficulty in analysis. 

Customer surveys should not be used to gather feedback into website user experiences. Asking users to recall their experiences of your website is likely to gather invalid data. 

It can be a challenge to code and analyse large sets of qualitative data. 

Gathering data from existing (or lapsed) customers will always have an element of bias, since these people have pre-conceptions of your brand / product / service based on their experiences. This is okay as long as you are aware of this and mitigate it accordingly, e.g. by also running research with people who have never heard of or used your brand / product / service before. For more focused research, in some cases using existing customers will be more relevant, whereas in others, using new users will be more appropriate.
customer-survey.considerations:
Tool
The survey could be built in a range of tools, including Google Forms, TypeForm, Survey Monkey, etc. There are plenty of free tools available for this activity, so there's not really any need to pay for a tool, unless you have more bespoke needs, e.g. large data sets, custom question logic, etc. 

Incentive
An incentive can be used to help boost the response rate. This could be in the form of a discount code or gift card. The amount and type of incentive should be determined by the type of people you are trying to reach, e.g. B2B vs. B2C, age, household income, job title / position, etc. 

Sample Size
You need approximately 200 open-ended responses to be confident in the strength of signal within the analysis (have a 95% confidence that the answer strength of the signal is valid within ~5-10% of what is reported).

customer-interviews.name: Customer Interviews
customer-interviews.desc: Usually 30 minute - 1 hour sessions run on a one-to-one basis either in person or remotely on Zoom, Teams, etc. Customers are recruited via email database and should ideally be incentivized for their time, e.g. a discount code or gift card.
customer-interviews.use:
To understand customers motivations, FUDs (fears, uncertainties, and doubts) perception of your product/service, to understand what problem/s your product/service solves for them and any improvement areas based on their experiences. 

Customer interviews can also be used to investigate specific topics or areas of opportunity.
customer-interviews.pros: Customer interviews allow you to dig deeper than customer surveys by asking follow up questions based on customers answers. This makes them more appropriate for more complex use cases or when you have a more specific area of focus.
customer-interviews.cons:
Customer interviews can be time-consuming, which means they are not effective for gathering large samples of data (unless you have a large budget / a lot of time resources). To help mitigate this, customer interviews can be used alongside a customer survey to gather both in-depth, high quality insights at a large scale. 

An insightful customer interview is determined by the questions you ask. Much like running moderated usability studies, there is skill involved in 
running an effective customer interview. You need to avoid leading questions, and also ensure questions are not multifaceted as this can cause difficulty in analysis. 

Customer interviews should not be used to gather feedback into website user experiences. Asking users to recall their experiences of your website is likely to gather invalid data. If you're looking for UX insights, a moderated usability study would be more appropriate (note: these methods can also be combined into a hybrid interview with some usability study tasks). 

Gathering data from existing (or lapsed) customers will always have an element of bias, since these people have pre-conceptions of your brand / product / service based on their experiences. This is okay as long as you are aware of this and mitigate it accordingly, e.g. by also running research with people who have never heard of or used your brand / product / service before. For more focused research, in some cases using existing customers will be more relevant, whereas in others, using new users will be more appropriate.
customer-interviews.considerations:
Recruitment 
The most effective recruitment method for existing customers is to reach out to your existing email database of customers. You should consider the types of customers you want to speak to when deciding who to email, e.g. recent convertors, loyal customers, lapsed customers, etc. Who you speak to will influence the output, so this should be based around your research goal. If you're running top-level exploratory research, then start with recent convertors, however if you are running interviews with a more focused objective, use this to determine who you reach out to. 

Incentive
An incentive can be used to help boost the response rate. This could be in the form of a discount code or gift card. The amount and type of incentive should be determined by the type of people you are trying to reach, e.g. B2B vs. B2C, age, household income, job title / position, etc. Also consider what you are asking of them, e.g. 30 minutes or 1 hour, the incentive should be reflective of the time they are giving you. 

Logistics
If you're recruiting customers for interviews and planning the sessions yourself, there are a few logistics to keep in mind;

- Booking a timeslot; before you send the initial email asking for people to take part, consider how you'll organise the sessions. You could share a Calendly link or something similar to allow customers to book directly with you. Whatever you use, you want to avoid having to manually agree on a date / time by going back and forth via email. 

- Tool; if you're not including any usability study tasks in your interview then you can effectively use any video conferencing tool (Zoom, Teams, Hangouts, etc). Don't forget to record the sessions (but ask permission first) to ensure you don't have to write everything down when you're running the interview. 

- No shows; especially when recruiting yourself, there's a relatively high chance of no-shows. Consider how to mitigate this, for example, sending out a series of reminders in the days / hours running up to the session, as well as over recruiting (e.g. running 1-2 more sessions than you need). Mention in your comms that you will wait for 10 minutes before assuming a no-show, so you don't have to sit and wait for the full amount of time until they turn up.

on-site-polls.name: On-site Polls
on-site-polls.desc: On-site polls are very short surveys that appear on your website for website users to answer. They are typically made up of 1-2 questions (since it is important not to disrupt the user journey). These can be open or closed questions, depending on the research objective. On-site polls can be run site wide or on specific pages, and can be triggered on a range of behaviours such as time on site / page, scroll depth and exit intent (on desktop).
on-site-polls.use:
Gather feedback as users are experiencing a website to help understand key barriers from users who haven’t converted yet. This makes them an effective method for gathering insight into UX friction and barriers to conversion. On-site polls can also be used to understand more about external factors, such as intent or motivation for visiting the website, or to understand more about the types of people visiting the website.

You can also be creative with the way you use on-site polls; for example you could use an on-site poll to recruit users for other research methods such as interviews or usability studies. This can be particularly useful when looking to target users who have a genuine need for your product or service, but who have not yet converted.
on-site-polls.pros:
On-site polls provide insight from users who have naturally found their way to your website, meaning they have a genuine need for your product or service. 

By their nature, on-site polls allow you to gather insight there and then while the user is interacting with your website. This means feedback is almost immediate and prevents the user having to recall their previous experiences (which can introduce a lot of bias).
on-site-polls.cons:
The main downfall of on-site polls is the disruption they can cause to the user experience. By appearing potentially mid-way through their journey, a poll could frustrate or disrupt, which could negatively impact brand perception and likelihood to convert. This can be somewhat mitigated by using logical poll design, e.g. making the pop up relatively subtle, using colours that match the website look and feel, etc. You should also consider what other pop ups you may have on your website. If you already have other pop ups such as offers, live chat, etc. then adding another pop up could exacerbate users frustration. 

The response rate is often relatively low. When planning your poll you should expect less than 10% response rate. You need to look at your current traffic levels and poll triggers to determine how long your poll will need to run. If you're going to have to run a poll any longer than 4 weeks to reach a minimum of 200 responses, then a poll may not be the most suitable research method for you.

The nature of on-site pop ups (and their propensity to cause frustration) can sometimes mean a high amount of "spam" responses. This means users who simply answer to get rid of the pop up, or answer saying "this pop up" is their main frustration (don't be surprised to see some swear words within the responses!) Review your responses and filter out any spam before ending a poll, ensuring you have reached your sample size with quality responses.
on-site-polls.considerations:
Questions / Logic 
There are different ways to approach on-site poll question design. Some schools of thought suggest that asking an "easy" question first, such as a closed Y/N question, can help "hook" users into answering more open questions. For example, "Can you find all the information you're looking for on this page?". However, in reality, there is often a large drop-off in response rate between the first and any subsequent questions. You need to consider the impact of this, e.g. you may come away with only insight on the % of users who answered Yes and No, which is not necessarily actionable. 

As such, you may wish to start with a more open question. This may reduce overall response rate but increase the quality of the insight, e.g. "What information, if any, is missing from this page?". But again, by asking this, you won't gather the top-level data on no. of Yes or No responses. 

An effective method is to run a series of polls. E.g. start with "Can you find all the information you're looking for on this page?". Then, once you have gathered sufficient data, run a second poll "What information, if any, is missing from this page?" It may be that a high percentage of respondents answered the first poll with "Yes", which could suggest that the information on the page is sufficient and efforts may be best used elsewhere.  

Tools 
Hotjar is one of the most popular tools for running on-site polls, due to its relatively cost-effective pricing model (although this has changed somewhat over recent months). There are many tools available with differing capabilities. When considering a tool the main factor to think about is the triggering capabilities; you want flexibility in who and how you target the poll to ensure you gather the most relevant insights. 

Sample Size
We need approximately 200 open-ended responses to be confident in our strength of signal within the analysis (have a 95% confidence that the answer strength of the signal is valid within ~5-10% of what is reported).

session-recordings.name: Session Recordings
session-recordings.desc: Session recording analysis involves watching recordings of real users interacting with the website, using a tool added into your website code. Recordings show the pages users view, where they scroll and click, and their mouse movements. It's also possible to see things like "rage clicks" where a user clicks on something multiple times in frustration.
session-recordings.use:
Session recordings can provide you with insight into real user's on-site behaviour which can help you identify areas of friction, frustration or barriers to conversion. 

Observing session recordings can be beneficial for gathering an overall understanding of how users are interacting with your website, as well as digging into interactions with specific pages or elements. 

Session recordings can also be used to watch users interacting with any live experiments. This can be beneficial from a QA and an analysis perspective.
session-recordings.pros:
Observe real user behaviour with no research bias; users don't specifically know they are being recorded. 

Helps bring other data such as digital analytics numbers "to life", by providing a more visual representation of the data. For example, Analytics might show a high exit rate from the basket page, session recordings can help explain why this is happening by showing users interacting with the basket (and potentially experiencing issues).
session-recordings.cons:
Session recordings are open to interpretation, since there's a lack of explanation of the behaviour. You may see someone doing something, but you won't necessarily know why they are doing that (and you can't ask them). 

Session recording analysis can be time-consuming, since you have to manually watch the recordings. There are ways to reduce this, such as speeding up recordings, skipping periods of inactivity and using filters to ensure you only watch the recordings that are most relevant to your research needs.
session-recordings.considerations:
Analysis & Interpretation
The primary consideration with session recording analysis is how to approach the analysis part. Typically one person within a team would watch either a set number of recordings or spend a set amount of time watching recordings. Although multiple people could also conduct this activity, perhaps focusing on different pages, elements or user type. It is important to establish a strategy for tagging and note-taking that is used consistently to support analysis and prevent insights from getting lost or diluted. 

For example, say you're watching 100 recordings. You might see some behaviours in the first 5 recordings that don't appear to be particularly interesting, but after 80 recordings you see that this behaviour actually happened in the large majority of sessions you've watched. This is why it is important to tag all behaviours from the beginning (within reason). 

It can be beneficial to gather multiple people together for analysis and interpretation of behaviours. Once you've watched and tagged multiple recordings, get together with your team to share what you found and hypothesise about why this behaviour might be happening. Since there is no way of knowing the truth at this stage, it can help to have multiple points of view. 

Qualitative vs. Quantitative
Although strictly speaking, session recordings are a form of digital analytics and therefore quantitative in nature, given the time involved in watching individual sessions in order to truly pull quantitative data from this method, you can think of session recordings as qualitative and heatmaps as their quantitative counterpart. In a similar way to surveys being useful for gathering large quantities of data, and interviews being effective for gathering a smaller, but higher quality of insight. 

Tools
Tools include Hotjar, Content Square, Full Story and Microsoft Clarity. These tools have a very wide range of price points, typically Hotjar was the tool of choice due to it's reasonable price point, but this has increased in price more recently. Microsoft Clarity offers a free solution.

heatmaps.name: Heatmaps
heatmaps.desc: Heat maps visualise on-site behaviour by representing clicks, hover and mouse movement with colours overlaid on a screenshot of the pages of a website. In general red indicates an area of high engagement (either clicks, hovers, or mouse movement) and blue indicates "cold" areas of low engagement. Heat maps are generated by a tool added into your website code. Heat map tools include Hotjar, Content Square and Full Story.
heatmaps.use:
Visualise how users behave on specific pages on the website. Understand which elements on the page are drawing users attention and which are being missed. Dig deeper into friction points / engagement with specific pages/elements.

Heatmap analysis can be beneficial for gathering an overall understanding of how users are interacting with your website, as well as digging into interactions with specific pages or elements. 

Heatmaps can also be used to compare on-page behaviour between different variations of an experiment, which can be beneficial from an analysis perspective.
heatmaps.pros:
Visualise real on-page behaviour with no research bias; users don't specifically know they are being recorded. 

Helps bring other data such as digital analytics numbers "to life", by providing a more visual representation of the data. For example, Analytics might show a high exit rate from the basket page, session recordings can help explain why this is happening by showing users interacting with the basket (and potentially experiencing issues). 

Heatmaps are an amalgamation of group behaviour, e.g. they represent trends from a large sample of users. As such, you can analyse large scale user behaviour relatively easily.
heatmaps.cons:
Heat maps are open to interpretation, since there's a lack of explanation of the behaviour. You may see high or low engagement with a specific element, but you won't necessarily know why there is high or low engagement. 

Heat maps can be prone to technical issues. It's important to be aware of the types of issues that can occur, for example, usually the tool will take a screenshot of the page from the sample user and then overlay the data which represents 100s or 1000s of users on that screenshot. That screenshot may not be representative of exactly what every user sees. Dynamic elements can also cause technical issues with heat maps; e.g. you may see high engagement on the main homepage banner, but this could actually represent engagement with the main navigation drop-downs. It's important not to take everything you see as 100% truth, if you see something unusual or that you can't explain, it may be indicative of a technical issue that should be investigated.
heatmaps.considerations:
Analysis & Interpretation
As with session recordings, it can be beneficial to gather multiple people together for analysis and interpretation of heatmaps to hypothesise about why this behaviour might be happening. Since there is no way of knowing the truth at this stage, it can help to have multiple points of view. 

Tools
Tools include Hotjar, Content Square, Full Story and Microsoft Clarity. These tools have a very wide range of price points, typically Hotjar was the tool of choice due to it's reasonable price point, but this has increased in price more recently. Microsoft Clarity offers a free solution.

analytics-data-analysis.name: Analytics Data Analysis
analytics-data-analysis.desc: Analysis of website analytics data to determine overall performance, performance by segment, e.g. device, channel, user type, analysis of on-site behaviour or digging into the impact a specific element or piece of functionality has on performance and user experience.
analytics-data-analysis.use:
Understand overall on-site user behaviour with high levels of certainty (assuming no sampling) and the differences across key segments. 

Dig deeper into the performance and / or impact of a specific page, element, or area of the website.
analytics-data-analysis.pros: Analytics data is one of the most robust sources of data you can use to help you understand on-site engagement, interaction, and user behaviour. This is because this data is based on real user behaviour, without research bias, at a large scale.
analytics-data-analysis.cons:
Sampling issues can reduce the accuracy of your data, which can result in drawing false assumptions, making decisions based on flawed data, etc.

Analytics data will tell you what is happening on your site, but not why. As with session recordings and heatmaps, the data is also open to interpretation. 

Robust analytics data analysis is a skill. It can easily be misunderstood or misinterpreted.
analytics-data-analysis.considerations:
Configuration
Effective analytics data analysis is reliant on a robust tool configuration, ensuring the data you're looking at is accurate. Effective set up can be complex and requires in-depth tool knowledge, ideally from a developer or from someone with experience in setting up analytics tools. 

Analysis
As analytics data is open to interpretation it is important to keep analysis actionable. At times it is relevant to simply point out facts, e.g. x% of data comes from mobile devices. But from an optimisation perspective, we should be considering the "so what?", e.g. what does this tell us, what opportunities does this present, etc? 

Tools
There are many digital analytics tools available. Chances are the business you work in or with will already use one. Google Analytics (now GA4) is one of the most popular and most well-known tools. The transition from Universal Analytics to GA4 happened in 2023 which significantly changed the way GA works.

sales-customer-service-interviews.name: Sales / Customer Service Interviews
sales-customer-service-interviews.desc: Sales / Customer Support interviews involve running 30 minute to 1 hour sessions with members of the sales team and/or the customer service team, either in person or remotely on Zoom, Teams, etc. Team members are recruited via email, either directly or through a client point of contact. These interviews draw on the internal teams who interact with customers every day, uncovering customer motivations, FUDs and frictions. This tribal knowledge from sales and customer service can then be applied to improve the website.
sales-customer-service-interviews.use:
Sales / Customer Support interviews are an effective method when running exploratory research. 

Sales interviews can be particularly useful when looking to develop or enhance ideal customer profiles, or personas. Speaking to sales teams can help you understand customers (and potential customers) key triggers and motivations for seeking out your product or service. You can also use sales interviews to uncover the primary barriers to conversion; the reasons why potential customers don't convert. 

Customer support/service interviews are effective when looking to understand customer's key issues or frustrations. This type of data can be useful when focusing on retention for subscription products/services. This activity can also identify key questions that users have that could be answered on the website.
sales-customer-service-interviews.pros:
Interviews allow you to dig deeper than surveys by asking follow-up questions based on answers. This makes them more appropriate for more complex use cases or when you have a more specific area of focus. 

Running interviews with Sales / Customer Support teams provides you with a snapshot of the top customer problems from an internal perspective.
sales-customer-service-interviews.cons:
There could be some bias in this data, given that it is internal data (and could be a negative reflection on internal teams).

competitor-review.name: Competitor Review
competitor-review.desc:
A competitor review involves reviewing the website UX of your competitors, using the UX heuristic principles,  to help gather an understanding of the market/industry, identify trends, gather inspiration and compare the user experience to the client’s website. 

A competitor review could also include review of the competitor's offering, pricing and overall proposition, to gather an understanding of the industry and identify opportunities.
competitor-review.use:
A competitor analysis can be beneficial to understand the different user experiences your potential customers may be exposed to in their comparison process. 

If you're struggling to solve a specific problem that is very specific to your industry, it can be beneficial to understand how others in your industry solve these problems.

If you're new to a role / industry then a competitor review can be beneficial to give you an overview of the industry and the competition. It's good practice to keep up to speed with what competitors are doing, but it should not side track you from focusing on solving your own business challenges.
competitor-review.pros:
Understand the wider industry, who is doing what and where you sit within this (from a UX, price, offering and proposition perspective). 

Gather ideas and inspiration about how to tackle key customer problems.
competitor-review.cons: Just because a competitor is doing something, does not mean it is working for them. It is important not to blindly copy competitors, but to use the insights as inspiration.
competitor-review.considerations:
Which competitors? 
You can include as many competitors as you have time for in your competitor review. Typically, we would review between 3-5. You may also want to consider including companies outside your "typical" competitor set, but who offer a solution to a shared customer problem, or have similar challenges (even if they are actually in a different industry/sector).
