ux-heuristic-review.name: UX Heuristic Review
ux-heuristic-review.desc: A UX heuristic review in this context is a review of a website based on a set of guiding UX principles, with the aim to identify areas of potential UX friction (ultimately areas of the user experience that could be creating friction or barriers for users on that website). A UX Heuristic review can be conducted on any digital experience; from a full website or core user journey, through to a single page, a piece of functionality, or a design or prototype.
ux-heuristic-review.use: A UX heuristic review is a good starting point for an experimentation programme or larger research project. This is a particularly effective option in the case of low traffic pages which making it difficult to run polls or analyze analytics data. A UX heuristic review can also be used when there's limited time / budget to run alternative user research activities.
ux-heuristic-review.pros:
A good starting point, particularly if you’re not very familiar with the website, e.g. you’re new to a business or working in an agency.

It’s relatively quick and inexpensive (no tool costs, only resource costs).

Can be used as an effective tool for encouraging collaboration across teams, and for helping build a culture of experimentation.

Identifies “low hanging fruit” such as bugs and JDIs.
ux-heuristic-review.cons:
Low strength of signal; insights aren’t based on real user data (therefore should not be used to validate high-risk business decisions).

Can be misused to push personal agendas, personal opinions, etc.

Additional research is (ideally) needed to support/validate insights.
ux-heuristic-review.considerations:
There are two steps involved in conducting a robust heuristic review; a group workshop and a scoring exercise conducted by a smaller team. 

The group workshop is a great way to gather insights from a wide range of people in a short period of time. This is an effective way to help avoid personal opinion; as the workshop will focus on identifying the themes that come up across individuals and groups. 

We recommend running the workshop with up to 10 people for between 1 hour and 1 hour 30 minutes. Assuming the workshop is being run remotely, you can use a tool like Miro or FigJam to run the workshop, if you're running it in person, you can use post-it notes instead. 

Example agenda; 
- Background & Intro - 10 mins
- Group breakout sessions:
          Part 1 (solo review, note taking & classification) 20 mins
          Part 2 (discuss & agree top 3) 10 mins
- Each group present back top 3-5 / group discussion - 20 mins

Next, is the scoring matrix. This is where a smaller project team dig further into the detail. This can also help validate what was discovered in the workshop. This involves up to 5 people scoring the user experience in a spreadsheet against a set of UX guidelines (see example in Resources).

card-sorting.name: Card Sorting
card-sorting.desc: Card sorting involves participants sorting and labeling website content (which is represented on "cards") into groups that make sense to them. The data from all participants can then be combined to identify the core groupings, labels, and any anomalies. This data can be used to inform the structure of a website's navigation.
card-sorting.use:
Card sorting is a core part of designing and developing a website from scratch. 

Card sorting can also be an effective research technique when other research has pointed to issues with how website content is grouped and labeled. This can help identify how users would expect content to be labeled and grouped, which can uncover optimization opportunities.
card-sorting.pros:
Card sorting is a relatively unique research method due to its focused nature (specifically focused on website content structure). 

Card sorting provides insight into how users expect website content to be grouped and labeled. 

You have the option of using open, closed, or hybrid card sorts, which can be beneficial in different ways at different points in a project. 

Tools like OptimalWorkshop make remote card sorting relatively quick and easy to set up and run.
card-sorting.cons:
Data analysis can be difficult/time intensive. The data provided by tools like OptimalWorkshop is extensive and although can be very insightful, it takes some understanding of the data to accurately interpret it. 

Remote-moderated / Moderated card sorting is time-intensive and could be expensive.
card-sorting.considerations:
Open vs. Closed
There are two different types of card sorting; open and closed. An open card sort. An open card sort allows participants to group and label all of the content as they wish, with no restrictions. A closed card sort involves participants grouping content under labels that you define. An open card sort therefore tends to be a more effective starting point. As you get closer to a defined set of labels, a closed card sort can be used to validate that users understand what content they would find under the labels you've defined. You can also use a hybrid approach where you define some category labels, but allow participants to also create their own. This can be beneficial when there are some categories that can't be changed for legal or technical reasons. 

Sample Size
Card sorting is primarily a quantitative method, and as such the sample size should be treated accordingly. NNGroup recommends 15 participants as a minimum, however, if you plan to run a quantitative style analysis then more is recommended.

Remote, Remote-moderated, Moderated
Card sorting can be conducted in various ways, similar to usability studies (Remote, Remote-moderated, Moderated). The benefit to Remote-Moderated or Moderated is that you are able to gather some qualitative insights as well as the data on the final groups and labels. For example, you'll be able to see when a participant is unsure where to group or how to label, you can find out what is making them unsure. This insight can highlight the content that could be most difficult to find an intuitive home for within the website structure. 

Tools
For remote or remote-moderated, there are a wide range of online tools available. OptimalWorkshop specializes in card sorting and tree testing, but you can also use tools such as Userlytics and Usabilityhub. The benefit of a tool like OptimalWorkshop is the extensive data available for analysis. For moderated card sorting you can either set up a computer and have participants conduct the card sort on a screen using one of these tools, or, you can use physical tools, e.g. post-it notes and pens. Using physical tools has the benefit of the participant feeling more free to move cards around, try different labels, etc. however, the data analysis is more challenging as you'd need to manually add the results from each participant into a tool in order to access the data. Moderated card sorting is also much more time intensive.
resources: Card sorting, uncover users' mental models (NN/g)

tree-testing.name: Tree Testing
tree-testing.desc: Tree testing involves replicating a website navigation (existing or proposed) in a link "tree". Recruited participants are then set tasks to find specific content or information within the link tree. This provides data on how easy specific content is to find within the navigational structure.
tree-testing.use:
Tree testing is similar to card sorting in that it provides insight into the navigational structure of a website. 

It can be used to gather initial data into where the main issues are within an existing navigational structure (as identified via other research methods), and it can also be used as a validation technique to validate changes/improvements.
tree-testing.pros:
Tree testing is a relatively unique research method due to its focused nature (specifically focused on website content structure). 

Tree testing provides insight into how easy content is to find within an existing or proposed navigational structure.

Tree testing can be done on existing structures to identify issues and opportunities or on proposed structures to validate changes. 

Tools like OptimalWorkshop make tree testing relatively quick and easy to set up and run.
tree-testing.cons: Data analysis can be difficult/time intensive. The data provided by tools like OptimalWorkshop is extensive and although can be very insightful, it takes some understanding of the data to accurately interpret it.
tree-testing.considerations:
Sample Size
Tree testing is primarily a quantitative method, and as such the sample size should be treated accordingly. There isn't a one-size-fits all number; instead the right number is based on the level of precision needed. Most tree tests have between 50-150 participants.
resources: Tree testing, fast iterative evaluation of menu labels (NN/g)

five-second-test.name: 5 Second Test
five-second-test.desc: We use a sample pool of target participants and analyse their responses to a series of questions after they look at a page for a limited time (typically 5 seconds). This helps us gather feedback on the copy, UI, clarity/motivation on next action etc. Five second tests allow us to gauge what information and impression users derive from a design within the initial five seconds of viewing the page. This helps us understand the effectiveness of the design and the messaging.
five-second-test.use:
The primary use case for a 5 second test is to gather insight into users very first impression of a page. This could be as part of research on landing page optimisation and / or acquisition research. 

5 second testing could also be used as part of validation research. If you want to establish how a change to a page, such as a headline copy change, will change users first impressions. 

5 second tests are best for gathering insights about copy and overall page design / messaging.
five-second-test.pros: 5 second testing is a quick and inexpensive way to gather insight into users first impressions of a page.
five-second-test.cons:
The nature of a 5 second test means there's only so much value you can gain. 5 seconds is not a long time, and it's likely the participant will only be able to answer 1 or 2 core questions. 

5 second tests are conducted on screenshots / designs, meaning participants can't interact with functionality.
five-second-test.considerations:
Tools
There are many tools that provide 5 second tests as a service, including Usabilityhub and Maze.

Sample Size
Ideally, each test would have about 50 -100 participants to maintain the quality of insights. The number of participants can increase or decrease depending on the number of segments of users you are targeting (ex: mobile and desktop tests require at least 50 participants each).

Length
It is possible to increase the length of a 5 second test, e.g. to 10 or 15 seconds. In some cases it could be beneficial to slightly increase the length of time the participant sees the page for, to ensure they have adequate time to answer the follow up questions effectively.

preference-test.name: Preference Test
preference-test.desc: Preference testing involves showing participants two (or more) versions of a page, an element, or a piece of copy, and asking them to select their preference and provide rationale for their preference. Data from the full sample of participants can then be used to draw conclusions about the best-performing version.
preference-test.use: Preference tests are a validation technique designed to gather data on a concept or solution. As such, preference tests can be beneficial in the planning stages of an AB test to either pre-validate or refine test concepts. Preference tests can also be used as an alternative to an AB test where true AB testing isn't possible for technical reasons or where there's not enough traffic.
preference-test.pros: Preference testing is generally quick and inexpensive, providing a quick and easy way to gather data to help inform concept design.
preference-test.cons:
Participants can't interact with functionality in a preference test. This means feedback is focused on the design, look and feel of the page, rather than being a true assessment of ease of use. This makes the method more suitable when the required feedback is based on the design or page copy, rather than the functionality or ease of use. 

Despite similarities with a true AB test, preference testing is subject to some research bias, since participants are not truly visiting your website or parting with their data/money. 

The low time investment from participants and thus the low level of incentive can impact the quality of the responses. It's important to review any qualitative feedback to help identify void responses.
preference-test.considerations:
Sample Size
Preference tests gather quantitative data, as such the sample size should be large enough to draw robust conclusions. We would recommend including at least 30 participants (ideally more). 

Tools
There are many preference testing tools. Typically this is an option built into tools like Maze, Usabilityhub and Wynter, rather than there being stand-alone tools. Maze and Usabilityhub are focused on design preference tests, whereas Wynter is focused on copy preference tests.

moderated-usability-studies.name: Moderated Usability Studies
moderated-usability-studies.desc: Use a sample pool of participants who match your target audience. Watch and listen as they walk through your site and perform queued tasks. Moderated usability studies involve one-to-one sessions conducted by a skilled moderator who will set the tasks and questions, allowing for a deeper level of insight. Moderated usability studies can be conducted in person or via Zoom, Teams, etc.
moderated-usability-studies.use: A requirement to understand the wider user journey, e.g. how users shop / browse more generally. A need for more in-depth, qualitative insights, a longer / more detailed user journey / set of tasks (that would be difficult to explain in a remote setting).
moderated-usability-studies.pros:
Moderated usability studies give more control to the moderator, since they are running the session live. This means they can answer questions from the participant and / or bring the participant back on track if they get stuck or misunderstand the task.

The insights from moderated usability studies tend to be more in-depth than those from remote. Again, this is because the moderator is able to ask follow-up questions, ask for clarification, etc.
moderated-usability-studies.cons:
The success of moderated usability studies is dependent on the skills of the moderator. Sessions can be subject to bias if moderators ask leading questions or tasks. 

Sessions can also be subject to bias such as the Hawthorne effect, since the participants are being observed live.
moderated-usability-studies.considerations:
Tool
There are many remote usability study tools, with slightly different capabilities and pricing models. Much like with AB testing tools, the success of your research is not necessarily determined by the tool you use, but by what you do with it (e.g. accurate recruitment, well-crafted tasks, and questions, etc). Key considerations when picking a tool include; the size and quality of their participant panel, the ability to add a recruitment screener, the analysis capabilities, what's included (e.g. participant incentives). Also double check how their pricing works, e.g. does it scale up based on the recruitment criteria and estimated length of session. Most tools now offer the option to set up and recruit for moderated usability studies in a similar way to remote; you will specify the moderator's availability and suitable participants will book in to the available slots. 

Recruitment
For moderated usability studies, a tool like Userlytics or Usertesting.com is not always necessary. You can use another recruitment method and use  any video call tool to run the sessions. Alternative recruitment methods include recruiting from existing customer database, or recruiting via an on-site poll. But be careful, as doing it this way increases the chance of no-shows, it also requires some admin from your side in terms of booking in sessions and paying incentives. 

Sample Size
Nielsen Norman says "The answer is 5, except when it's not" regarding usability study sample size. We use this as a guide; but one that should be considered rather than followed blindly. For example, if you're testing on multiple devices or with different user types, then you need to apply this rule to all of those segments. You may also want to add 1-2 additional "buffer" sessions to account for poorer quality participants, tech issues, no shows, etc.
resources: How to get the most out of your user testing efforts

copy-testing.name: Copy Testing
copy-testing.desc: A form of user research focused on website copy and written content. A sample pool of users are recruited and asked to review excerpts of copy. They are then asked to answer a series of questions to assess their level of understanding, outstanding questions and next steps. Our recommended copy testing tool is Wynter.
copy-testing.use:
Understand how your audience perceives your messaging
- Is anything confusing or unclear? 
- Is there something that doesn’t make sense or misses the mark? 

Validate your audience’s pain points. 
- Do they feel your company understands their needs and solves their problems? 

Define the benefits that resonate the most with your audience.
- What benefits are they most interested in? 
- What benefits are they least interested in? 

Stand out from the competition
- You can identify if the headline resonates with the target audience, if they find it unique or bland.
copy-testing.pros:
You can outsource the participants, meaning that you don’t need:
- to implement any new tools on your actual website. 
- a lot of visitors on your site, or existing customers to get started.

Gather qualitative feedback on the website copy and content.

Recruit people who match your ICP.
copy-testing.cons: Copy testing is focused only on copy, you can't / shouldn't use this method to gather insights about design or functionality.
copy-testing.considerations:
Recruitment
You need to consider who is your target audience and ensure that the participants match your ICP. You should evaluate if the tool you are going to use will help you find relevant participants in the right audience, or if you can find those participants elsewhere.
resources: How does product copy format affect user engagement (original research)

prototype-testing.name: Prototype Testing
prototype-testing.desc: Use usability study tools or specific prototype testing tools such as Maze to set recruited participants specific tasks to complete on a prototype version of a page, functionality or website. This is usually conducted remotely (see remote usability studies) but can also be in a moderated setting.
prototype-testing.use: To validate that a proposed solution has the intended impact in improving the user experience. Identify any issues pre-development.
prototype-testing.pros:
Gather qualitative data to support a design or functionality change before (or instead of) AB testing.

Prototype testing is beneficial when you can't AB test due to technical restrictions or traffic limitations. 

Prototype testing tools tend to be relatively inexpensive.
prototype-testing.cons:
Creating a prototype for testing can be time-intensive, depending on the functionality you're testing. 

If you're going on to AB test as well running prototype testing will slow down the process of getting test results. 

Technical issues with the prototype during the sessions can negatively impact the validity of the insights. 

As with usability studies, you need to consider the wording used in your questions and tasks, to prevent leading participants and invalidating your insights.
prototype-testing.considerations:
Tools
You can use any usability study method or tool to run prototype testing, such as remote, remote moderated, moderated, Userlytics, Usertesting.com, etc. You can also use a specific prototype testing tool, such as Maze. 

Sample size
The same logic as usability studies applies here. Nielsen Norman says "The answer is 5, except when it's not" regarding usability study sample size. We use this as a guide; but one that should be considered rather than followed blindly. For example, if you're testing on multiple devices or with different user types, then you need to apply this rule to all of those segments. You may also want to add 1-2 additional "buffer" sessions to account for poorer quality participants, tech issues, no shows, etc.

diary-studies.name: Diary Studies
diary-studies.desc: Diary studies involve recruiting participants to take part in research over the period of a few weeks to a few months. Participants are asked to submit "diary" entries every time they naturally do a certain behaviour, e.g. browse for a specific product or service. Diary studies can be conducted via email, text, whatsapp or bespoke platforms.
diary-studies.use:
Used to collect qualitative data about user behaviors, activities, and experiences over time. This is appropriate only in cases where the decision making process is particularly long, and there is a need to understand the wider user journey / key touchpoints.

Relevant sectors could be the automotive or property industries. Diary studies could also be effective when looking to gather insight into offline parts of the journey, e.g. the returns process.
diary-studies.pros: Diary studies are a in-depth longitudinal research study, as such you can gather robust data about the wider user journey and decision-making process. These insights are difficult to gather using any other method.
diary-studies.cons:
Diary studies can be long and complex to conduct. The exact length will depend on the typical decision-making process, e.g. buying a car or a house. 

Diary studies can be expensive since you need to recruit carefully (people who are genuinely in the market for these products or services) and incentivize generously (since these participants could be part of the research study for weeks or months).
diary-studies.considerations:
Incentives
It is advisable to think about offering a staged incentive. E.g. 50% upfront, 50% on completion. This ensures participants continue engaging with the research project all the way through. 

Tools
There are many tools you could use to gather "diary entries" on an ongoing basis. You could use text, Whatsapp, or email. Alternatively use a specific diary study tool. The key consideration here is to use a method that is as easy as possible for the participant to input an entry, if they have to log into a specific tool everytime, they may be less inclined to submit an entry vs. using Whatsapp.
resources: Diary studies, understanding long-term user behaviour (NN/g)
When to use context methods, field and diary studies (NN/g)

ads-analysis.name: Ads Analysis
ads-analysis.desc: Analysis of ads data within Google Ads, Facebook ads, Instagram ads, etc, focused on performance, CPC, Impressions, Clicks, Cost, with the aim of identifying which campaigns and ads are underperforming.
ads-analysis.use:
Increase your ROI from acquisition spend
Improve the effectiveness of paid landing pages
Start optimising acquisition activities
Connect your acquisition strategy to your on-site optimisation efforts
ads-analysis.pros: Analysing your ads data helps you to optimise spend by highlighting which campaigns are performing well, and which are not.
ads-analysis.cons: Ads analysis on its own lacks qualitative insight needed to really determine why certain efforts are not performing.
ads-analysis.considerations:
Expertise
Ideally, you need someone with acquisition knowledge to conduct this activity, at the same time, you want someone who isn't directly involved in your acquisition strategy, to prevent bias.

live-chat-analysis.name: Live Chat Analysis
live-chat-analysis.desc: Analysis of on-site live chat transcripts to uncover fears, uncertainties and doubts that users are facing on-site, including identifying any unanswered questions (which could point towards missing or sub-optimal website content).
live-chat-analysis.use:
If you have live chat on-site and get high volumes of engagement, then analysing the questions users are asking can be a goldmine of insights.

If you have limited time and budget to conduct new research then analysing live chat data is a really effective way to tap into users main queries and struggles.
live-chat-analysis.pros:
No need to conduct new research / collect data & insights. 

Gather insights from real users who have a genuine need for your product or service. 

Understand the key questions and barriers holding users back from converting.
live-chat-analysis.cons: Can be time-consuming if you have a lot of data to analyse; equally, the value can decrease if you have limited data.
live-chat-analysis.considerations:
Sample Size 
As with surveys and polls, the sweet spot for analysis of live chat data is between 200-300 responses. 

Live Chat type
The value of this data will depend on the type of live chat you have. E.g. a chatbot vs. a manned live chat. How you approach analysis will depend on what data you collect and in what format, for example, if the customer service team categorise the query or not.

win-loss-analysis.name: Win-loss Analysis (CRM Analysis)
win-loss-analysis.desc: Analysis of data housed within existing CRM (Customer Relationship Management) tool / database, e.g. Salesforce, Pipedrive, etc. to understand customers and potential customers challenges, pain points, blockers, decision making process, etc. on a large scale and identify nuances between different customer types.
win-loss-analysis.use:
Lack insight into ICPs specific motivations, pain points, FUDs. 
Struggling to convert leads into paid customers. 
Messaging and content is informed by internal assumptions, opinions, etc. rather than data and insight. 
Have difficulty effectively communicating the value proposition, what problems you solve for businesses, etc. 
Need to build ICPs and personas from scratch to help inform wider marketing efforts.
win-loss-analysis.pros:
No need to conduct new research / collect data & insights. 

Gather insights from real users who have a genuine need for your product or service. 

Understand the key questions and barriers holding users back from converting.
win-loss-analysis.cons:
Can be difficult to conduct effectively if CRM data is not well organised, record is not kept of sales conversations, reasons for not converting, etc.

May be subject to some bias if based solely on notes from sales team within CRM.
win-loss-analysis.considerations:
Sample Size
In this case sample size will depend on the amount of data you have, which will relate to the number of leads, prospects, customers, etc. It will also depend on the depth of the data. If you only have top level data, then aim for more (200-300), whereas if you have detailed, more qualitative data, then you could aim lower 50-100 responses. Also consider the different segments within your sample if you're including convertors and those who did not convert, you need an appropriate sample size for both / all segments.

form-analytics.name: Form Analytics
form-analytics.desc: Form analytics is similar to regular analytics analysis, but focused on your website forms.  You can analyse metrics such as form field interaction, drop out rates, error rates, etc to understand which fields are causing friction.
form-analytics.use: Exploratory research has identified a specific barrier in your checkout or on other onsite forms.
form-analytics.pros: Provides in-depth data to inform form optimisation; e.g. removing fields, changing layouts etc.
form-analytics.cons: Can be subject to technical issues, much like standard analytics tools, the accuracy of the configuration is integral.
form-analytics.considerations:
Tools
You can either set this up manually using custom analytics tracking or using a bespoke Form analytics tool, like Zuko.
resources: How to fill the form optimization knowledge gap
Form optimization tips with Alun from Zuko

ab-testing.name: A/B Testing
ab-testing.desc: Running a live, randomised experiment that splits traffic between a control and one or more variants to measure the causal effect of a change on a target metric.
ab-testing.use: Confirming that a change actually improves the outcome it targets before rolling it out fully. Settling disagreements about a design or flow with real customer behaviour rather than opinion.
ab-testing.pros: Gives a direct, causal read on impact rather than a proxy signal. Removes bias from the decision since real customers self-select into each path.
ab-testing.cons: Needs enough traffic and time to reach a reliable result. Only tests the specific variants built, so it depends on earlier research to shape a strong hypothesis.
ab-testing.considerations: Best run once a hypothesis has already been shaped by exploratory and focus-stage research, since a test is only as good as the idea behind it.
resources: How to prioritize your A/B test ideas
Can you run multiple A/B tests at the same time

search-serp-analysis.name: Search & SERP Analysis
search-serp-analysis.desc: Analysis of organic search performance and the surrounding results landscape. The queries that bring visitors in and the ones that should but don't, rankings and click-through against the pages that hold them, and the content competitors use to win the intents that matter. Pairs the site's search data with the language customers actually type. Branded query volume belongs here too, since demand for the brand by name, tracked over time, is one of the few behavioural reads on brand awareness.
search-serp-analysis.use: Grow qualified organic traffic, close the gap between customer search language and site language, prioritise content investment by intent, and connect organic acquisition to on-site optimisation. Track branded search demand as a behavioural indicator of brand awareness, before and after brand-level changes.
search-serp-analysis.pros: Real behavioural data at scale from actual customer queries. Shows demand and competitive position without spending on a panel or media.
search-serp-analysis.cons: Intent has to be inferred from queries rather than asked. Rankings move slowly, so validating changes takes time and can be confounded by algorithm updates.

win-loss-interviews.name: Win-loss Interviews
win-loss-interviews.desc: One-to-one interviews with recent buyers and lost prospects about how the purchase decision actually went: the trigger that started the search, the alternatives weighed, the objections that nearly killed the deal, and what tipped it in the end. Run like customer interviews, but the sample deliberately includes the deals you lost, which is where the sharpest positioning insight lives.
win-loss-interviews.use: Understand why deals are won and lost in the buyer's own words. Feeds ICP research, positioning and messaging with the market's real decision criteria and vocabulary, and locates the funnel stages where deals stall or die. Adds the why behind the patterns CRM win-loss analysis surfaces.
win-loss-interviews.pros: Covers the buyers you lost, whose reasons never surface in customer research. First-hand accounts of the decision replace the sales team's secondhand recollection, and the buyer's own language feeds straight into positioning and messaging work.
win-loss-interviews.cons: Lost prospects are harder to recruit and often need a neutral interviewer plus a real incentive to speak candidly. Samples stay small, so the findings show the shape of the decision rather than its frequency.
win-loss-interviews.considerations:
Recruitment
Reach out within a few weeks of the decision, while the detail is still fresh. Lost prospects speak more honestly to a neutral third party than to anyone from the vendor, so consider who conducts the sessions. A meaningful incentive matters more here than in customer research, since lost prospects owe you nothing.

Sample size
Qualitative goals apply: a handful of wins and a handful of losses per segment is a workable guide, and the losses are usually where the sharpest insight sits. Pair with CRM win-loss analysis when the pattern needs scale behind it.

brand-perception-survey.name: Brand Perception Survey
brand-perception-survey.desc: A structured survey run with a recruited panel that matches the target market, measuring unaided and aided brand awareness, brand preference, and the associations people hold against named competitors. Run before and after a brand change, the same instrument becomes a tracker. The baseline wave shows where perception stands, and later waves show whether it moved.
brand-perception-survey.use:
Establish a brand baseline before a rebrand, relaunch or repositioning, then re-measure after it ships.
Find out whether the target market knows the brand exists, and what it is known for.
See how perception and preference compare against named competitors in the consideration set.
Track awareness and perception over time as a standing programme measure.
brand-perception-survey.pros:
Recruited panels reach the people who don't know you, which the customer list never can, so awareness numbers stay honest.

Everything is measured against named competitors, so position is relative rather than absolute.

Repeatable. The same instrument re-run later gives a genuine before-and-after comparison.
brand-perception-survey.cons:
Panel quality decides everything. A panel that doesn't match the real buying audience measures the wrong people's opinions.

Perception moves slowly, so waves need spacing before the deltas mean anything.

It says what the market thinks, not what to change. It needs qualitative methods alongside it to explain the numbers.
brand-perception-survey.considerations:
Sampling
Survey the target market, not the customer base. Existing customers already know the brand, which inflates awareness and skews perception toward the product experience. Customers can be a separate, clearly labelled slice if their view is also wanted.

Consistency
The value of tracking comes from asking the same questions of the same profile every wave. Resist rewording between waves, because every change breaks the comparison.

Timing
Run the baseline before the brand change is announced, and leave enough time after launch for the market to notice before re-measuring.

social-media-listening.name: Social Media Listening
social-media-listening.desc: Systematic monitoring of what people say about a brand, its competitors and its category across social platforms, forums and communities. It captures the unprompted voice of the market: the words people use, the complaints and praise they volunteer, and how the conversation shifts over time.
social-media-listening.use:
Hear how the market talks about the brand and its competitors when nobody is asking.
Surface the vocabulary customers use for the category, to feed messaging and search work.
Watch how conversation volume and sentiment shift around a launch, rebrand or incident.
Find where the audience actually gathers, which for technical audiences is often forums and communities rather than mainstream platforms.
social-media-listening.pros:
Unprompted and continuous, so there is no interviewer effect and no survey fatigue.

Covers competitors as easily as the brand itself.

Picks up shifts quickly, where structured research only catches them at the next wave.
social-media-listening.cons:
The people who post are not a representative sample of the market, and loud voices skew the read.

Volume can be thin for niche and B2B categories, so weeks can pass without meaningful signal.

Sentiment classification is rough. Irony, jargon and mixed opinions get mislabelled.
social-media-listening.considerations:
Where to listen
The right sources depend on the audience. Developer and technical audiences live in forums, communities and Q&A sites more than mainstream social platforms, so pick sources by where the buyers actually talk, not by what the tool covers best.

Baseline before judging
Raw mention counts mean little on their own. Track against a baseline period and against competitors so a change reads as signal rather than noise.

online-review-analysis.name: Online Review Analysis
online-review-analysis.desc: Structured analysis of the reviews the market has already written on review platforms, app stores and marketplaces, for the brand and for its competitors. Mining the text surfaces recurring praise, complaints, feature language and switching triggers, in the reviewers' own words.
online-review-analysis.use:
Learn the strengths and weaknesses the market volunteers about the brand and its competitors.
Harvest the vocabulary reviewers use, for messaging, copy testing and search work.
Spot the recurring reasons people switch toward or away from a product.
Build competitor understanding without recruiting a single participant.
online-review-analysis.pros:
The data already exists, so it is fast to start and there is no recruitment.

Competitor reviews are as accessible as your own, which is rare in research.

Reviewers explain their reasoning in their own words, giving quotable, specific language.
online-review-analysis.cons:
Reviews cluster at the extremes, because the satisfied middle rarely writes.

Platform incentives and vendor review programmes shape what gets posted.

Reviews describe the product experience more than the brand, so they inform perception work without measuring awareness.
online-review-analysis.considerations:
Source selection
Match platforms to the category. Software lives on software review sites, consumer products on marketplaces and app stores. Note each platform's review-collection incentives when weighing what you read.

Recency
Weight recent reviews more heavily. Old reviews describe a product and a market that may no longer exist.

outcomes.name: Acquisition
outcomes.metric: Traffic quality, cost per acquisition, ROAS
outcomes.desc: Getting the right visitors to the site efficiently, and making sure the promise that brought them matches what they find.

outcomes.name: Conversion
outcomes.desc: Turning visitors into customers once they arrive, by removing friction and answering the questions that hold them back.

outcomes.name: Retention
outcomes.metric: Retention rate, churn, repeat rate, LTV
outcomes.desc: Keeping customers active and getting enough ongoing value to stay, and understanding why they leave when they do.

outcomes.name: Foundational
outcomes.metric: Not a metric in itself; underpins all three areas
outcomes.desc: Cross-cutting understanding such as ICP, audience and messaging that feeds acquisition, conversion and retention rather than sitting under one of them.

northStar: The one measurable outcome the programme is accountable to. It stays fixed while the opportunities and bets beneath it flex as research and test learnings come in. Set this per client; everything below ladders up to it.

acquisition-research.name: Acquisition Research
acquisition-research.problem: I clicked the ad expecting one thing, the page doesn't match it, so I leave.
acquisition-research.opp: Paid visitors bounce off landing pages
acquisition-research.hmw: How might we make the landing page deliver on the promise the ad made?
triggers: High ad spend with weak ROAS, high landing-page bounce, poor message match between the ad and the page.
acquisition-research.desc:
Paid traffic is arriving but converting poorly, and it is unclear whether the problem sits in the ads, the landing pages, or the match between the two. This recipe connects acquisition spend to the on-site experience so you can improve ROAS rather than simply cut budget.

Ads analysis and analytics data analysis set the quantitative picture: which campaigns and channels underperform, and what those visitors do once they land. A UX heuristic review flags likely friction on the landing pages, and a 5 second test reveals whether the first impression and message match the promise made in the ad. The data shows where the leak is, the qualitative methods suggest why, and optimisation effort lands on the right page with the right message.
stages: Set the quantitative picture: which campaigns underperform, and what those visitors do once they land.
Flag likely friction on the landing pages themselves.
Check the first impression matches the promise the ad made.

conversion-research.name: Conversion Research
conversion-research.problem: Something keeps stopping me finishing what I came to do, but it's not one obvious thing.
conversion-research.opp: Visitors fail to convert across the site
conversion-research.hmw: How might we find and remove the biggest on-site barriers to conversion?
triggers: Below-benchmark conversion rate, no single clear drop-off, need to build a prioritised test pipeline.
conversion-research.desc:
You need a complete view of where and why visitors fail to convert across the site, not just on a single page. This is the broad diagnostic that feeds an experimentation programme.

It deliberately triangulates across data types. Analytics data analysis, heatmaps and session recordings give the quantitative behavioural picture of where users drop off. Customer surveys and on-site polls add the voice of the customer: the motivations, fears and barriers behind that behaviour. Remote usability studies show real people attempting core journeys, and a UX heuristic review provides an expert read to anchor and prioritise. No single method is trusted on its own; the value comes from where the behavioural, attitudinal and observed evidence agree.
stages: Build the quantitative behavioural picture and an expert baseline.
Add the voice of the customer behind the behaviour.
Watch real people attempt the core journeys.

saas-pricing-page.name: SaaS Pricing Page
saas-pricing-page.problem: I can't work out which plan is right for me or what I'd actually end up paying, so I stall.
saas-pricing-page.opp: Buyers can't tell which plan fits them
saas-pricing-page.hmw: How might we help buyers self-select the right plan with confidence?
triggers: High exit on the pricing page, low trial-to-paid, sales repeatedly answering the same plan-comparison questions.
saas-pricing-page.desc:
The pricing page is where SaaS buyers decide whether the product is worth it, and it is often where they stall. The goal is to understand why visitors hesitate, what they need in order to feel confident, and whether the plans, copy and layout match how they actually evaluate value.

Start broad with a competitor review and a UX heuristic review to see how rivals frame pricing and to surface obvious friction on your own page. Sales and customer service interviews bring in the real objections and questions buyers raise, which often explain hesitation the page never addresses. Copy testing checks whether plan names, feature descriptions and value framing are understood by the target audience. Remote usability studies then show how people move through the page and where they get stuck choosing a plan. The combination moves from market context, to internal knowledge, to message clarity, to observed behaviour, so no single lens carries the decision.
stages: See how rivals frame pricing and surface obvious friction on your own page.
Bring in the real objections buyers raise, and check the plan language is understood.
Watch how people move through the page and where they get stuck choosing.

b2b-icp-research.name: B2B ICP Research
b2b-icp-research.problem: Nothing on the site convinces me it's built for a company like mine.
b2b-icp-research.opp: We don't really understand our ICP
b2b-icp-research.hmw: How might we speak to our ICP's real motivations, triggers and doubts?
triggers: Messaging built on internal assumptions, unclear persona definition, weak win rates against competitors.
b2b-icp-research.desc: Messaging and targeting are running on assumptions about who the ideal customer is and what drives them. This recipe builds a grounded picture of the ICP: their motivations, triggers, and fears, uncertainties and doubts. The picture starts in the CRM record, where win-loss analysis shows who actually buys and who walks. The interviews go deep, the polls add immediacy and scale, and the usability sessions tie attitude to behaviour. The messaging built on all of it then gets tested with the people it describes before it ships.
stages: Get the real language and hesitations behind a decision to buy, from the CRM record and the buyers themselves.
Capture intent and barriers from people evaluating you right now, and tie attitude to behaviour.
Test the messaging built on it with the people it describes before it ships.

landing-page-optimisation.name: Landing Page Optimisation
landing-page-optimisation.problem: I clicked the ad expecting one thing, the page doesn't match it, so I leave.
landing-page-optimisation.opp: Paid visitors bounce off landing pages
landing-page-optimisation.hmw: How might we make the landing page deliver on the promise the ad made?
triggers: High ad spend with weak ROAS, high landing-page bounce, poor message match between the ad and the page.
landing-page-optimisation.desc:
A landing page is underperforming and you need to understand what is blocking visitors before redesigning it. The aim is to diagnose friction across first impression, message and on-page behaviour.

A 5 second test and a UX heuristic review give a fast read on clarity and obvious friction. Heatmaps and session recordings show where attention goes and where people hesitate or drop off. On-site polls ask visitors directly what is missing or unclear, and copy testing checks whether the core message lands with the target audience. The behavioural data shows what is happening, the polls and copy testing explain why, and the heuristic review and 5 second test surface quick wins to act on first.
stages: Get a fast read on clarity and obvious friction.
See where attention goes, where people drop, and ask them what's missing.
Confirm the winning change with a live experiment.

checkout-cart-optimisation.name: Checkout & Cart Optimisation
checkout-cart-optimisation.problem: I was ready to buy, then the checkout asked for too much or felt unsafe, so I bailed.
checkout-cart-optimisation.opp: Shoppers abandon at the payment step
checkout-cart-optimisation.hmw: How might we get ready-to-buy shoppers through checkout without losing them?
triggers: High cart abandonment, drop-off concentrated on the payment or shipping step, repeated 'is this secure' support queries.
checkout-cart-optimisation.desc: Shoppers add items to the basket and then leave before paying, and the team can't see what tips them out. Start broad to find where value leaks. Analytics shows which checkout steps lose the most people, while session recordings and heatmaps show what those people actually do at the moment they drop. Then focus in on the payment and address fields with form analytics, and ask leavers why with an exit poll. Finish by validating a reworked flow in remote usability sessions before it goes near a build, so several independent signals point at the same fix.
stages: Find which steps lose the most people, and watch what they do at the moment they drop.
Zoom into the payment and address fields, and ask leavers why.
Prove the reworked flow with observed tasks and a live test.

navigation-information-architecture.name: Navigation & Information Architecture
navigation-information-architecture.problem: I know what I want but the menus don't match how I think, so I keep hunting.
navigation-information-architecture.opp: Visitors can't find the right product or page
navigation-information-architecture.hmw: How might we structure navigation around how customers actually look for things?
triggers: Heavy reliance on site search, high pogo-sticking between category pages, low findability scores in past tests.
navigation-information-architecture.desc: Visitors know what they want but can't find it, so they bounce between pages or fall back on search and give up. Begin by reading the symptoms. Analytics surfaces the search terms and dead-end paths, and session recordings show the hunting behaviour in context. Then move to the structure itself, using card sorting to learn how customers expect content grouped and tree testing to check whether a proposed menu lets them find things. Validate the winning structure in usability sessions so you change the navigation on evidence rather than on internal logic.
stages: Read the symptoms: search terms, dead-end paths, hunting behaviour.
Learn how customers expect content grouped.
Check the proposed structure lets people find things.

validating-redesign.name: Validating a Redesign Before Build
validating-redesign.problem: As a visitor I'd be handed a new design the team hopes is better but hasn't checked with anyone like me.
validating-redesign.opp: A redesign is about to ship untested
validating-redesign.hmw: How might we prove the new design beats the current one before we build it?
triggers: Major redesign scoped, significant build cost, no evidence the new direction outperforms the current page.
validating-redesign.desc: A big redesign is about to be built and the risk is shipping months of work that performs worse than what it replaces. This recipe front-loads the validation. A five second test checks whether the new design communicates its point at a glance, a preference test weighs it against the current version, and copy testing pressure-tests the words carrying the message. Prototype and moderated usability sessions then confirm people can actually complete the core tasks, so the redesign earns its place before a developer touches it.
stages: Check the new design communicates its point, and pressure-test the words carrying it.
Weigh it against the current version, confirm people can complete the core tasks, then prove it live.

churn-retention.name: Churn & Retention Research
churn-retention.problem: I signed up but stopped getting enough value to justify keeping the subscription.
churn-retention.opp: We don't know why customers churn
churn-retention.hmw: How might we understand and reduce the reasons customers leave?
triggers: Rising churn, low repeat usage, cancellation reasons citing value or fit.
churn-retention.desc: Customers cancel and the business is left guessing whether it was price, value, a missing feature or a bad experience. Start with the traces customers leave behind. Analytics shows where usage tails off before a cancellation, CRM and win-loss data show patterns in who leaves, and live chat logs surface the complaints that recur. A cancellation survey then quantifies the leading reasons, and interviews with churned customers explain the why behind the numbers. The layers turn a vague churn figure into specific, addressable causes.
stages: Read the traces customers leave behind: usage, CRM patterns, recurring complaints.
Quantify the leading reasons, then hear the why in customers' own words.

value-prop-messaging.name: Value Proposition & Messaging
value-prop-messaging.problem: I'm on the page but I can't tell what this is or whether it's for someone like me.
value-prop-messaging.opp: Visitors don't understand what we offer
value-prop-messaging.hmw: How might we make our value clear and relevant within seconds of landing?
triggers: High bounce on key landing pages, low message-clarity scores, sales correcting basic misunderstandings.
value-prop-messaging.desc: Visitors land on the site and can't quickly tell what the product is, who it's for or why it beats the alternative. The explore work goes to the source. Interviews and surveys capture how customers describe the value in their own words, and a competitor review shows which claims are table stakes and which are genuinely differentiating. That language then gets sharpened and tested, with copy testing and a five second test checking whether the message reads clearly and fast, and on-site polls confirming the page answers the questions real visitors arrive with.
stages: Capture the value in customers' own words, and map which claims differentiate.
Sharpen and test whether the message reads clearly and fast.
Confirm the page answers the questions real visitors arrive with.

mobile-experience.name: Mobile Experience Optimisation
mobile-experience.problem: On my phone the site is fiddly, so I give up and mean to come back later, but I don't.
mobile-experience.opp: Mobile converts far worse than desktop
mobile-experience.hmw: How might we close the gap between mobile and desktop conversion?
triggers: Mobile conversion well below desktop, high mobile share of traffic, mis-tap and zoom behaviour in recordings.
mobile-experience.desc: Mobile traffic is large but converts well below desktop, and the team can't tell whether it's layout, speed, forms or intent. Begin by isolating the mobile segment in analytics to size the gap and locate it, then watch mobile session recordings and heatmaps to see the cramped taps, mis-hit buttons and scrolling that numbers alone hide. Form analytics exposes where mobile input breaks down, and an on-site poll catches frustrations in the moment. Validate fixes in usability sessions run on real devices, not a shrunken desktop window.
stages: Isolate the mobile segment to size the gap, then watch what the numbers hide.
Expose where mobile input breaks down, and catch frustrations in the moment.
Test fixes in sessions run on real devices.

product-page.name: Product Page Optimisation
product-page.problem: I looked at the product but couldn't get the answers I needed to commit, so I left it.
product-page.opp: Product views don't turn into add-to-carts
product-page.hmw: How might we give product pages the information and reassurance that earns the add-to-cart?
triggers: High product-page traffic with low add-to-cart rate, repeated pre-sales questions, attention stopping above key content.
product-page.desc: People reach the product page but don't add to basket, and it's unclear whether the blocker is information, doubt or price. Analytics shows how product pages perform relative to each other and where attention stops, while recordings and heatmaps reveal which content people seek out, skip or expand. On-site polls and a short survey draw out the unanswered questions and hesitations that hold a purchase back. Usability sessions then confirm whether a revised page actually resolves them, so the changes address real doubt rather than guesswork.
stages: Compare product-page performance and see where attention stops.
Draw out the unanswered questions and hesitations.
Confirm the revised page resolves real doubt.

lead-gen-form.name: Lead-Gen Form Optimisation
lead-gen-form.problem: I started filling in the form but it asked too much or broke, so I stopped.
lead-gen-form.hmw: How might we make the lead form quick and painless enough to finish?
triggers: Low form completion rate, drop-off on specific fields, high cost per lead from paid traffic.
lead-gen-form.desc: Prospects start the lead form but abandon it before submitting, and the cost of every lost completion is high. Form analytics is the spine here, showing the exact fields where people stall, re-enter or quit, and session recordings add the behaviour around those fields. Analytics frames how many are affected, and an on-site poll asks what stopped them. A shortened or restructured form is then checked in usability sessions before launch, so the changes are grounded in where the friction genuinely sits.
stages: Locate the exact fields where people stall, and frame how many are affected.
Watch behaviour around those fields, and ask what stopped them.
Check the restructured form in usability sessions before launch.

onboarding-activation.name: Onboarding & Activation Research
onboarding-activation.problem: I signed up but couldn't quickly see the point, so I never really got started.
onboarding-activation.opp: New users don't reach first value
onboarding-activation.hmw: How might we get new users to their first win before they lose interest?
triggers: High signup-to-activation drop-off, low day-7 return rate, early support tickets about getting started.
onboarding-activation.desc: New users sign up but never reach the first moment of real value, so they drift away before the product can prove itself. Analytics maps the activation funnel and the step where new users stall, and session recordings show what they try and abandon in those early minutes. Interviews and a survey explain what people expected and where reality fell short, while diary studies capture the experience across the first days rather than a single visit. Usability sessions on the onboarding flow then confirm whether a revised path gets people to value faster.
stages: Map the activation funnel and watch the early minutes where users stall.
Learn what people expected, and follow the experience across the first days.
Confirm a revised onboarding path gets people to value faster.

trust-credibility.name: Trust & Credibility Audit
trust-credibility.problem: It looks interesting but I'm not sure I can trust them with my money or my details.
trust-credibility.opp: Visitors hesitate because they don't trust us yet
trust-credibility.hmw: How might we give visitors enough confidence to commit?
triggers: High traffic with low conversion on commitment steps, weak or missing proof elements, low brand familiarity.
trust-credibility.desc: Visitors are interested but hesitate to commit because the site hasn't earned their confidence yet. A heuristic review flags the credibility gaps an expert eye catches quickly, such as thin proof, weak security cues or vague claims, and a competitor review shows the trust signals buyers see elsewhere in the category. Interviews, a survey and on-site polls then locate the specific doubts that stall real customers, and copy testing checks whether reassurance language actually lands. Together they separate the trust problems you can feel from the ones customers act on.
stages: Flag credibility gaps an expert eye catches, and map the trust signals buyers see elsewhere.
Locate the specific doubts that stall real customers.
Check the reassurance language actually lands.

researching-low-traffic.name: Researching With Low Traffic
researching-low-traffic.problem: We don't have the volume to be statistically significant, so every change is a leap of faith.
researching-low-traffic.opp: We can't test because traffic is too low
researching-low-traffic.hmw: How might we build evidence for decisions when traffic can't support A/B tests?
triggers: Sessions too low to reach significance in a realistic test window, high-stakes pages with thin behavioural data, polls and analytics too sparse to read, decisions resting on opinion or the loudest voice.
researching-low-traffic.desc:
The site doesn't get enough traffic to run reliable A/B tests or gather meaningful poll and analytics data, so decisions default to opinion. This recipe builds evidence with methods that bring their own participants instead of borrowing yours.

A UX heuristic review and a competitor review set an expert baseline and show how others in the category solve the same problems, with no traffic required. Recruited-panel methods then carry the focus work: remote usability sessions show real people from your audience attempting the core journey, and copy testing checks the message lands with the people it is written for. Preference and prototype tests stand in for the A/B test at the validation step, weighing a proposed change against the current version with a recruited sample. The result is a decision backed by several independent signals, none of which needed the traffic you don't have.
stages: Set an expert baseline and see how the category solves the same problems. No traffic required.
Let recruited panels carry the work: your audience, someone else's traffic.
Stand in for the A/B test with recruited-sample comparisons.

category-listing-page.name: Category & Listing Page Optimisation
category-listing-page.problem: I'm scrolling the category page but nothing helps me narrow it down, so I leave without picking anything.
category-listing-page.opp: Shoppers browse categories but don't click into products
category-listing-page.hmw: How might we help shoppers narrow the range and find a product worth clicking?
triggers: High category-page exits, low listing-to-product click-through, filters and sorting applied then abandoned, deep scrolling with few product clicks.
category-listing-page.desc: Shoppers reach the category and listing pages but leave without clicking into a product, and it is unclear whether the range, the filters or the product cards are to blame. Analytics sizes the problem first, showing which categories leak the most and how listing visits relate to product views. Heatmaps and session recordings then reveal how people actually work the page: what they filter and sort, how far they scroll, and which product cards earn attention. An on-site poll asks browsers what is stopping them narrowing down. Usability sessions validate a revised listing experience against real find-and-choose tasks, so changes to filters, sorting and card content follow the way shoppers genuinely shop the range.
stages: Size the problem: which categories leak most, and how listing visits relate to product views.
Watch how people work the page, and ask what's stopping them narrowing down.
Test a revised listing experience against real find-and-choose tasks.

trial-to-paid.name: Free Trial to Paid Conversion
trial-to-paid.problem: I tried it during the trial but never hit the moment that made paying feel worth it.
trial-to-paid.opp: Trial users don't convert to paid
trial-to-paid.hmw: How might we make the value obvious enough during the trial that paying feels like the natural next step?
triggers: Low trial-to-paid rate, trial usage tailing off mid-trial, upgrade prompts ignored, discount requests clustering at trial end.
trial-to-paid.desc: People sign up for the trial but never convert to a paid plan, and the team can't tell whether the product failed to prove its value or the upgrade moment failed to land. Analytics maps what trial users actually do, separating those who convert from those who drift, and session recordings show the early sessions where the difference takes shape. Win-loss analysis of the CRM adds the pattern across accounts that upgraded and accounts that lapsed. An end-of-trial survey quantifies the leading reasons for not converting, and interviews with expired trials explain the gap between what people expected and what they experienced. Together these separate a value problem from a pricing or timing problem, which point to very different fixes.
stages: Map what trial users actually do, and watch the early sessions where converts and drifters diverge.
Quantify why trials lapse, and hear the expectation gap in users' own words.

traffic-quality-channel-fit.name: Traffic Quality & Channel Fit Research
traffic-quality-channel-fit.problem: The ad pulled me in but the offer wasn't what I actually wanted, so I left.
traffic-quality-channel-fit.hmw: How might we attract visitors who match our best customers?
triggers: High traffic with low qualified-lead rate, poor fit between ad audience and ICP, weak engagement from paid channels.
traffic-quality-channel-fit.desc: Traffic is growing but the visitors arriving aren't the ones the business is built for, and everything downstream pays for it. This recipe works out where the misfit traffic enters and what it costs. Behavioural data shows which sources send visitors who bounce, stall or never return, CRM data shows which sources actually produce customers, the ads layer shows which campaigns and queries are buying the mismatch, and the sales floor tells you what a wrong-fit visitor sounds like. Panel message testing then checks that sharpened targeting and positioning reach the right people before more media spend follows the fix.
stages: See which sources send visitors who engage and which send visitors who vanish, and which actually produce customers.
Name the campaigns and queries buying the mismatch, and hear what a wrong-fit enquiry sounds like.
Test the sharpened who-this-is-for message before spend follows it.

content-to-lead.name: Content-to-Lead Conversion Research
content-to-lead.problem: The article was useful. I read it, got what I needed and left. Nothing made a next step feel worth it.
content-to-lead.opp: Organic visitors read the content and leave
content-to-lead.hmw: How might we turn content readers into subscribers and leads without wrecking the reading experience?
triggers: Content traffic grows steadily while lead volume stays flat
Strong rankings and high entrances on posts with near-zero CTA engagement
The newsletter and gated offers barely grow despite real readership
content-to-lead.desc: The content programme is doing its job of attracting readers, and then the relationship ends at the last paragraph. This recipe finds where the reader-to-lead path breaks. Analytics shows which posts attract visitors with any buying intent and where readers exit, heatmaps show whether the calls to action are even seen on the templates readers actually use, and on-site polls ask readers directly what they came for and what would make a next step worthwhile. Testing offer and CTA framings on a panel, then checking they register at a glance, de-risks the fix before it ships across hundreds of posts.
stages: Find which posts attract buying intent and where readers exit.
Ask readers what they came for and what would make a next step worth it.
Test offer and CTA framings, then check they register at a glance.

lead-quality.name: Lead Quality Research
lead-quality.problem: I downloaded the guide because it looked useful. I was never going to buy anything.
lead-quality.opp: The pipeline fills with leads sales can't close
lead-quality.hmw: How might we attract fewer, better-fit leads instead of more of the wrong ones?
triggers: Lead targets get hit while pipeline and revenue stay thin
Sales rejects, recycles or quietly ignores a large share of handed-over leads
Gated content fills the CRM with students, researchers and job-seekers
lead-quality.desc: The lead count looks healthy and the pipeline doesn't, which usually means the acquisition engine is optimised for volume rather than fit. This recipe diagnoses the gap from both ends. CRM analysis separates the sources, campaigns and offers that produce closed-won customers from the ones that produce noise, and structured input from the whole sales team turns "the leads are junk" into specific, recurring rejection patterns. Interviews with recent well-fit buyers establish what a good lead actually looked like on the way in. Panel testing then checks that requalified messaging and offers attract the buyer and politely lose the browser.
stages: Separate the sources that produce customers from the ones that produce noise, through the CRM and the sales floor.
Hear the decision firsthand, from well-fit buyers and the deals that got away.
Check requalified messaging attracts the buyer and politely loses the browser.
lead-quality.opp2: We don't really understand our ICP

seo-search-intent.name: SEO & Search Intent Research
seo-search-intent.problem: I searched for exactly the thing they do. They weren't there, so I went with someone who was.
seo-search-intent.opp: The people searching for what we solve don't find us
seo-search-intent.hmw: How might we show up for the searches our best customers are already making, in their words rather than ours?
triggers: Organic traffic is concentrated on branded terms
Competitors hold the rankings for the problem-language queries
Content ranks for informational terms that never convert
seo-search-intent.desc: The customers who most need what the business does are searching for it in their own words and finding someone else. This recipe closes the language gap between how customers describe the problem and how the site describes the solution. Search data shows which intents the site is absent from and which rankings never earn the click, interviews surface the vocabulary customers actually use, and a review of the winning results pages shows what earning each intent takes. A glance test on the landing experience then confirms the click pays off before content investment scales. Search intent match is message match's organic twin.
stages: Map which intents the site is absent from and which rankings never earn the click.
Learn the words customers use for the problem, and see who owns each intent today.
Confirm the landing page pays off the query at a glance.

involuntary-churn.name: Involuntary Churn & Payment Recovery Research
involuntary-churn.problem: My card expired and the subscription just stopped. I never decided to leave, and nothing brought me back.
involuntary-churn.opp: Subscriptions end on failed payments, not decisions
involuntary-churn.hmw: How might we catch and recover the customers who never chose to churn?
triggers: Churn reporting doesn't split voluntary from involuntary
A chunk of cancellations show no engagement decline beforehand
Support keeps fielding "why was I cancelled" and "can't update my card" tickets
involuntary-churn.desc: A meaningful slice of churn is customers who never decided to leave; a payment failed, the retries ran out, and the subscription ended for someone who wanted to keep it. This recipe sizes and explains that leak. Payment funnel analysis shows where charges fail and how many recover, CRM analysis shows who lapses this way and what they were worth, and support logs surface the billing friction customers hit when they try to fix it themselves. A survey of lapsed involuntary customers answers the question the data can't: did they even know, and what would have caught it. Recovery messaging and the update-payment flow get tested before they carry the fix.
stages: Size the leak: where charges fail, how many recover, and what those customers were worth.
Surface the billing friction customers hit, and ask lapsed customers whether they even knew.
Test the recovery messaging and the update-payment flow before they carry the fix.

engagement-decay.name: Engagement Decay & Habit Research
engagement-decay.problem: I liked it at first. Then life got busy, I stopped opening it, and nothing gave me a reason to come back.
engagement-decay.opp: Activated customers drift away after the early weeks
engagement-decay.hmw: How might we help the product earn a place in customers' routines after the novelty fades?
triggers: Activation numbers look healthy while week-four-plus retention slides
A wide gap between weekly and monthly active customers
Exit surveys say "just stopped using it" more than any specific complaint
engagement-decay.desc: These customers activated, found value, and then drifted; not because anything broke, but because the product never earned a place in the routine. Onboarding research won't catch this, because the loss happens after onboarding succeeds. Cohort analysis shows which behaviours separate the customers who stay from the ones who fade and when the fade starts. Diary studies then do what no analytics can: a week or two inside customers' real routines showing where the product fits, what competes with it, and what quietly replaces it. Interviews with drifted-but-recoverable customers explain what changed. Re-engagement and habit-hook concepts get prototype-tested before anything is built.
stages: Find which behaviours separate the customers who stay from the ones who fade, and when the fade starts.
Spend a week or two inside customers' real routines, then hear what changed from the drifters.
Prototype-test re-engagement and habit hooks before anything is built.

repeat-purchase.name: Repeat Purchase & Post-Purchase Research
repeat-purchase.problem: The first order was fine. Nothing after it gave me a reason to order again.
repeat-purchase.opp: First-time buyers never place a second order
repeat-purchase.hmw: How might we make the second order feel like the natural next step rather than a fresh decision?
triggers: Revenue leans almost entirely on new-customer acquisition
Repeat purchase rate stays flat while acquisition costs climb
The post-purchase programme is an order confirmation and not much else
repeat-purchase.desc: Most first-time buyers never come back, and the margin lives in the orders they never place. This recipe finds out why the second order isn't happening. Purchase cohort analysis shows the repeat rate, the typical gap to a second order, and which first products lead somewhere versus nowhere. The support team's structured input surfaces what buyers experience after checkout: delivery, returns, and the gap between the listing and the product in hand. One-time buyers explain why there was no second order, and repeat buyers explain what actually brought them back, which are rarely the same answer. Post-purchase and reorder concepts then get tested head to head with past buyers before the lifecycle programme is rebuilt around them.
stages: Read the repeat rate, the gap to a second order, and what buyers experience after checkout.
Ask one-time buyers why there was no second order, and repeat buyers what brought them back.
Test post-purchase and reorder concepts head to head with past buyers.

brand-perception-tracking.name: Brand Perception Baseline & Tracking
brand-perception-tracking.problem: I've heard the name, but I couldn't tell you what they do differently or whether they're for someone like me.
brand-perception-tracking.opp: We don't know how the market sees us
brand-perception-tracking.hmw: How might we know how our market actually perceives us, and whether that perception is moving?
triggers: A rebrand or repositioning is being scoped with no baseline of current awareness or perception
Positioning debates inside the company run on opinion because nobody has market evidence
Sales keeps correcting the same wrong assumptions about what the company does
The brand is missing from consideration sets it should be in
brand-perception-tracking.desc:
A rebrand, relaunch or repositioning is coming, and nobody can say how the market sees the brand today, which means nobody will be able to say whether the work changed anything. This recipe builds the baseline first so the after has a before.

The explore work reads what the market says unprompted. Social listening and review analysis surface the words people already use about the brand and its competitors, branded search demand shows how many go looking by name, and sales and support know which wrong assumptions keep recurring. A panel survey of the target market, rather than the customer list, then quantifies unaided and aided awareness, preference and perception against named competitors, while copy testing checks whether the intended positioning lands with the people it describes. Validation is longitudinal rather than a one-off check. The same survey, run against the same profile after the change, turns before and after from a feeling into a measurement.
stages: Read what the market says unprompted: conversations, reviews, and demand for the brand by name.
Quantify awareness, preference and perception against named competitors, and check the positioning language lands.
Re-run the same measurement after the change and compare to the baseline.
